module

public import Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Function.L2Space
public import Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Measure.Lebesgue.Basic

@[expose] public section

/-!
# Spectral sets

This file defines the basic notions used in problems related to spectral sets
and Fuglede's conjecture: translations, exponential characters,
spectral pairs, spectral sets, and translational tilings in Euclidean space.
-/

open Real Set Complex MeasureTheory
open scoped InnerProductSpace

/-- The translate of a set `Ω` by a vector `t`.-/
def translateSet {d : ℕ} (Ω: Set (Fin d → ℝ)) (t : Fin d → ℝ) :
    Set (Fin d → ℝ) :=
  {x | x - t ∈ Ω}

/-- The exponential character `x ↦ exp(2π i ⟪ξ, x⟫)`. -/
noncomputable def exponentialCharacter {d : ℕ} (ξ x : Fin d → ℝ) : ℂ :=
  Complex.exp (2 * π * Complex.I * (∑ i, ξ i * x i))

/-- The exponential character is continuous. -/
theorem continuous_exponentialCharacter {d : ℕ} (ξ : Fin d → ℝ) :
    Continuous (exponentialCharacter ξ) := by
  unfold exponentialCharacter
  continuity

/-- The exponential character has norm one. -/
theorem norm_exponentialCharacter {d : ℕ} (ξ x : Fin d → ℝ) :
    ‖exponentialCharacter ξ x‖ = 1 := by
  unfold exponentialCharacter
  have h_simp :
      2 * π * Complex.I * (∑ i, ξ i * x i) =
        Complex.I * ((2 * π * ∑ i, ξ i * x i) : ℝ) := by
    simp
    ring
  rw [h_simp, Complex.norm_exp_I_mul_ofReal]

/-- On a finite-measure set, every exponential character belongs to `L^2`. -/
theorem exponentialCharacter_memLp {d : ℕ} {Ω : Set (Fin d → ℝ)}
    (hΩ_finite : volume Ω ≠ ⊤) (ξ : Fin d → ℝ) :
    MemLp (exponentialCharacter ξ) 2 (volume.restrict Ω) := by
  rw [MeasureTheory.memLp_two_iff_integrable_sq_norm (continuous_exponentialCharacter ξ).aestronglyMeasurable]
  simp_rw [norm_exponentialCharacter]
  change IntegrableOn (fun _ ↦ (1 : ℝ) ^ 2) Ω volume
  simpa using
    (MeasureTheory.integrableOn_const (μ := volume) (s := Ω) (C := (1 : ℝ)) hΩ_finite)

/--
(Ω, Λ) is called a spectral pair if Λ is a spectrum for Ω, i.e.
a set Λ of frequencies such that the associated exponential characters
 form an orthogonal basis of L^2(Ω).
-/
def spectralPair {d : ℕ} (Ω Λ : Set (Fin d → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ hΩ_finite : volume Ω ≠ ⊤,
    let e : (Fin d → ℝ) → MeasureTheory.Lp ℂ 2 (volume.restrict Ω) := fun ξ ↦
      MeasureTheory.MemLp.toLp (exponentialCharacter ξ) (exponentialCharacter_memLp hΩ_finite ξ)
    (∀ ξ₁ ∈ Λ, ∀ ξ₂ ∈ Λ, ξ₁ ≠ ξ₂ → ⟪e ξ₁, e ξ₂⟫_ℂ = 0) ∧
    Submodule.topologicalClosure (Submodule.span ℂ (Set.range fun (ξ : Λ) ↦ e ξ.1)) = ⊤

/--
A set is spectral if it belongs to a spectral pair.
-/
def isSpectral {d : ℕ} (Ω : Set (Fin d → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ Λ : Set (Fin d → ℝ), spectralPair Ω Λ

/--
A set Ω tiles ℝ^d by translation if there exists a set T of translation vectors
such that the translates of Ω by T cover ℝ^d without overlap.
-/
def tilesByTranslation {d : ℕ} (Ω : Set (Fin d → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ T : Set (Fin d → ℝ), T.Countable ∧
    volume (Set.univ \ (⋃ t ∈ T, translateSet Ω t)) = 0 ∧
    (∀ {t₁ t₂ : Fin d → ℝ}, t₁ ∈ T → t₂ ∈ T → t₁ ≠ t₂ →
      volume (translateSet Ω t₁ ∩ translateSet Ω t₂) = 0)

findings.description: The definition requires finite volume but not positive volume or nonzero basis vectors. If `volume Ω = 0`, then `volume.restrict Ω = 0`, the L² space is the zero space, and both orthogonality and the dense-span condition hold for every frequency set Λ. In `/workspace/review/scratch.lean` I proved `volume Ω = 0 → spectralPair Ω Λ` for arbitrary Λ, without sorry. In particular, `spectralPair ∅ Set.univ` holds, and `isSpectral` declares every null set spectral. A nonempty family of zero vectors is not an orthogonal basis, and the standard spectral-set notion excludes zero-measure sets.
findings.source_evidence: KLM, Spectral sets and weak tiling, §1.1 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04540; v3 TeX), starts: “Let Ω ⊂ R^d be a bounded, measurable set of positive measure,” then defines a spectrum by an orthogonal basis of exponentials. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuglede%27s_conjecture likewise defines spectral sets and spectral pairs for sets with positive finite Lebesgue measure.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `0 < volume Ω` as a conjunct of `spectralPair`, retaining the existing finite-volume requirement. This makes every exponential nonzero in L² and repairs the inherited null-set behavior of `isSpectral`.

findings.description: No Lebesgue-measurability condition is imposed on Ω. For nonmeasurable inputs, Mathlib's restriction is not a way to enforce that condition: for finite outer measure it equals restriction to `toMeasurable volume Ω`. I proved `spectralPair (toMeasurable volume Ω) Λ ↔ spectralPair Ω Λ` under `volume Ω ≠ ⊤`, and the corresponding equivalence for `isSpectral`. This admits genuinely non-Lebesgue-measurable spectral sets. For example, take a Vitali selector V in [0,1] and Ω = [0,1] \ V. Every measurable subset of V is null, so restriction to Ω equals restriction to [0,1]; consequently the current predicate accepts the integer spectrum for Ω, although Ω is not Lebesgue measurable. This persists after adding positive volume.
findings.source_evidence: KLM §1.1 explicitly assumes Ω measurable (https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04540). GL16 §1 also begins with a bounded, measurable set of positive Lebesgue measure (https://arxiv.org/e-print/1602.08850). Mathlib's `MeasureTheory.Measure.restrict_toMeasurable`, in MeasureTheory/Measure/Restrict.lean, states equality of these restrictions for every finite-outer-measure set. The Vitali construction and its disjoint rational translates are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitali_set; the same disjoint-translate argument shows that every measurable subset of V is null.
findings.suggested_fix: Require `NullMeasurableSet Ω volume` in `spectralPair`, in addition to positive finite volume. This expresses Lebesgue measurability without unnecessarily restricting the reusable notion to Borel sets. `isSpectral` will inherit the corrected domain.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/Arxiv/2209.04540/SpectralSetsAndWeakTiling.lean, this theorem uses `spectralProductImpliesRightSpectral 1 m`. Mathlib's `ConvexBody` permits the singleton body `A = 0`, whose carrier is `{0}`. Then `A × B` has zero volume for every B and is automatically `isSpectral` under the current library definition. Thus the theorem asserts that every bounded measurable B is spectral. Taking m = 2 and B a nondegenerate triangle refutes it. I proved in Lean that, for every n > 0, the current helper is equivalent to spectrality of all bounded measurable right factors. This is not the solved cylinder theorem in GL16.
findings.source_evidence: KLM §1.1 defines convex bodies as compact convex sets with nonempty interior, and §7.2 records the n = 1 result (https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04540). GL16's main cylinder theorem concerns the positive-measure spectral-set convention; its introduction explicitly states that planar triangles are not spectral (https://arxiv.org/e-print/1602.08850). Mathlib Analysis/Convex/Body.lean requires only compactness, convexity and nonemptiness, and defines the zero body as a singleton.
findings.suggested_fix: Preferably repair `spectralPair` by requiring positive volume. Then spectrality of the product excludes degenerate left factors. Alternatively, explicitly require positive volume or nonempty interior of A in `spectralProductImpliesRightSpectral`. Keep the source's solved/positive-answer metadata; changing the answer would not repair the misstatement.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/Arxiv/2209.04540/SpectralSetsAndWeakTiling.lean, the quantified `ConvexBody (Fin 2 → ℝ)` can be the singleton `{0}`. Its product with any bounded measurable B is null, hence `isSpectral` by the current definition. The asserted positive answer therefore forces every such B to be spectral, contrary to the planar-triangle example. The problem relies on spectrality excluding null products, but the imported predicate does not do so.
findings.source_evidence: KLM §7.2 records the positive n = 2 result using convex bodies with nonempty interior, as defined in §1.1 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04540). GL20's main product theorem treats convex polygons under the positive-measure spectral-set convention (https://arxiv.org/e-print/1801.02164). GL16's introduction records that planar triangles are nonspectral (https://arxiv.org/e-print/1602.08850).
findings.suggested_fix: Require positive volume in `spectralPair`, or add a positive-volume/nonempty-interior hypothesis on A in the shared helper. The former repairs this theorem and the other product variants together.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/Arxiv/2209.04540/SpectralSetsAndWeakTiling.lean, this purported open question includes singleton left factors in R³. With A = {0}, its spectral-product hypothesis holds for every B because the product is null. Consequently its right-hand proposition reduces to the already-false assertion that every bounded measurable right factor is spectral; m = 2 and a planar triangle give a counterexample. This is a change to the mathematical question, not evidence that KLM's open problem has been solved negatively.
findings.source_evidence: KLM §7.2 asks about a convex body A in R^n, using the explicit nonempty-interior convention of §1.1, and says only n = 1 and 2 are proved (https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04540). The source's definition of spectrality requires positive measure. Nonspectral planar triangles are recorded in GL16 §1 (https://arxiv.org/e-print/1602.08850).
findings.suggested_fix: Repair the positive-measure requirement in `spectralPair`, or explicitly exclude zero-volume left factors in `spectralProductImpliesRightSpectral`. Do not replace the open answer by `False` on the strength of this degenerate counterexample.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/Arxiv/2209.04540/SpectralSetsAndWeakTiling.lean, the general product question inherits the same null-product error. The allowed choice n = 1, m = 2, A = {0}, and B a nondegenerate planar triangle makes the imported `isSpectral (productSet A B)` true and `isSpectral B` false. Thus the current universal proposition has an elementary negative answer unrelated to the intended convex-body product problem. The Lean experiment proves the stronger diagnostic equivalence: for any n > 0, `spectralProductImpliesRightSpectral n m` is equivalent to spectrality of every bounded measurable B in R^m.
findings.source_evidence: KLM §7.2 asks whether spectrality of A × B forces spectrality of B when A is a convex body; §1.1 explicitly requires nonempty interior for a convex body and positive measure for a spectral set (https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04540). Mathlib's `ConvexBody` does not require nonempty interior. GL16 §1 supplies the nonspectral-triangle example (https://arxiv.org/e-print/1602.08850).
findings.suggested_fix: Strengthen `spectralPair` to require positive volume. Alternatively, add `(interior (A : Set (Fin n → ℝ))).Nonempty` or `0 < volume (A : Set (Fin n → ℝ))` to the shared product helper. Repair the statement rather than its open-status metadata.

reformulations.difference: On the intended positive finite-measure, Lebesgue-measurable domain, the definition uses pairwise vanishing inner products and dense linear span, without separately asserting linear independence or countability of Λ.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Each character's squared L² norm is |Ω| > 0; the norm identity was checked in Lean. Thus orthogonality implies linear independence, and closure of the span being top is precisely completeness. Dividing the characters by sqrt(|Ω|) gives an orthonormal Hilbert basis. Countability is automatic: the Fourier transform of 1_Ω is continuous and nonzero near zero, while differences of distinct frequencies must be its zeros. Hence Λ is uniformly discrete and therefore countable. GL16 §2 gives this standard argument. The missing explicit conditions are consequently not additional defects on this domain.

reformulations.difference: The source's countable partition up to measure zero is expressed as a null uncovered set plus a null intersection for each pair of distinct translates, rather than pointwise uniqueness almost everywhere.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For countable T, the union of all pairwise-overlap exceptional sets is null. Outside that union and the uncovered null set, exactly one translate contains each point. Conversely, almost-everywhere unique membership implies both displayed null-set conditions. I proved the full equivalence with `∃ T, T.Countable ∧ ∀ᵐ x, ∃! t : T, x ∈ translateSet Ω t.1` in the scratch file. This matches KLM §1.1 and GL16's partition-up-to-null-sets convention.

reformulations.difference: The ambient `MeasurableSet Ω` condition selects Borel sets, whereas the literature allows Lebesgue-measurable bounded sets.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every bounded Lebesgue-measurable set has a bounded Borel representative equal to it almost everywhere. Spectrality depends only on the restricted measure, and a countable translational tiling is unchanged by null modifications because translations preserve null sets. The representative can be chosen inside a bounding box, preserving boundedness and positive volume. Thus this restriction does not change the universal conjecture.

        Complex.I * ((2 * π * ∑ i, ξ i * x i) : ℝ) := by
    simp
    ring
  rw [h_simp, Complex.norm_exp_I_mul_ofReal]

  simp_rw [norm_exponentialCharacter]

(Ω, Λ) is called a spectral pair if Ω is Lebesgue measurable with positive finite
measure and Λ is a spectrum for Ω: the associated exponential characters
form an orthogonal basis of L^2(Ω).
-/
def spectralPair {d : ℕ} (Ω Λ : Set (Fin d → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  NullMeasurableSet Ω volume ∧ 0 < volume Ω ∧
    ∃ hΩ_finite : volume Ω ≠ ⊤,

A set is spectral if it belongs to a spectral pair.
-/

A set Ω tiles ℝ^d by translation if there exists a set T of translation vectors
such that the translates of Ω by T cover ℝ^d without overlap.

      volume (translateSet Ω t₁ ∩ translateSet Ω t₂) = 0)
